new_statements.rule_in_words: GROUP-LEVEL ONLY: Connell (who collected the only modern Mbongno data, a 1995 wordlist) characterises all Mambiloid languages, Mbongno included in his comparison set, as having three or four level lexical tones. No source located says anything about word stress or accent in Mbongno; no phonological description of Mbongno exists (Glottolog: 0 grammar/phonology/sketch refs; Blench Atlas 2019 entry 316 'Refs.' empty; SIL archives 0 items). Blench 1993:111 likewise treats Mambiloid prosody purely in terms of tone ('exceptional for the complexity of its tonal systems and the prevalence of phonemic contour tones').
new_statements.domain_note: The quoted sentence is a family-level generalisation over Mambiloid, not a Mbongno-specific description; it concerns lexical tone inventory only. It should not be entered in the catalog as a Mbongno stress statement; it is recorded here as the closest first-hand prosodic statement covering the language.
new_statements.identity_note: Label cross-wiring to watch: Blench 1993:107 used 'Mbɔŋnɔ (= Magu)' for the language of Zongo Ajiya and 'Mvanɔ (= Kamkam)' for the language of Kakara, whereas Blench's Atlas ed. IV (2019), ISO 639-3 and Glottolog now have Mbongno [bgu, mbon1253] = Kamkam/Bungnu/Kakaba at Kakara (and 'Kamkam' in Cameroon, ALCAM) and Mvanip [mcj, mvan1238] = Magu at Zongo Ajiya. Older 'Magu'/'Kamkam' wordlists (Meek 1931; Williamson 1973 BCCW 'Kamkam = Mvanip') must therefore be checked village-by-village before being attributed to mbon1253. Connell reports Mbongno and Mvanip as mutually intelligible per Mbongno speakers.
